newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus talks backed by Security Council-Clerides.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus talks backed by Security Council-Clerides.

text.p: Greek Cypriots are attending settlement talks on the protracted Cyprus dispute, sponsored by the United Nations and set for July, after assurances the negotiations have the full backing of the Security Council, Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides said on Monday.

"We will attend the talks despite the fact we have not noticed any change in the Turkish stance on the basic aspects of the problem, but after assurances given by the United Nations Secretary-General that he will have the support of the five permanent members of the Security Council," said Clerides, president of the internationally recognised Greek-Cypriot-led government.

The U.N. has tentatively set a July 9 date to convene face-to-face talks between Clerides, as Greek Cypriot leader, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash. It will be their first known encounter in nearly three years.

The latest push for movement on the dispute comes amid heightened tensions on the divided island and a military buildup by the two sides, and ahead of the start of negotiations for Cyprus to enter the European Union, due to begin early in 1998.
Sir David Hannay of Britain is due in the Cypriot capital Nicosia on June 9 and 10 for talks with the two leaders ahead of the July summit.

Clerides told reporters an additional reason for attending the talks was that he did not want to appear to be spurning the Secretary-General's invitation, a move which could have an impact on Cyprus's bid to join the EU.
In an indirect reference to earlier statements by Rauf Denktash, Clerides said security was an issue of priority for the Greek Cypriots.
"Future security is one of the most basic issues and without finding a solution to this particular aspect no Cyprus solution can be reached," he said.

Some 30,000 Turkish troops are stationed in northern Cyprus, occupied in 1974 in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece. Turkey invaded citing its rights as a guarantor power.

Denktash, heading a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north recognised only by Ankara, last week said the aim of the talks should not be to water down guarantee agreements and replace the Turkish rights of guarantee by a multinational force.

The Greek Cypriots support the deployment of a multinational force with a Security Council mandate to intervene when the territorial integrity or security of one of the two communities on the island is threatened. It also seeks to abolish the right of intervention of guarantor powers.
Britain, Turkey and Greece are guarantor powers of Cyprus under agreements giving the former British colony independence.
